description: We are a group of Cooper Union students interested in space science, earth science, and biological science. We are super excited to participate in the Hackathon!
summary:
Exploration of Mars has produced some of the most compelling evidence suggesting the potential of life beyond Earth, namely the discovery of water on the now arid planet. 
As Mars research develops, the ability to understand and compare the two planets grows.  
In drawing parallels between Earth and Mars, we open the doors to incredible research and mission opportunities.

This was the inspiration for TerraMatch.

TerraMatch is a data-driven comparison system that evaluates four extreme Earth environments—the Aralkum Desert, McMurdo Dry Valleys, Lut Desert, and Salar de Uyuni—against data from the Gale Crater collected by NASA’s Curiosity rover.

Using NASA Earth-observation data and rover measurements, we created a similarity index to compare thermal, atmospheric, radiation, mineral composition, and astrobiological makeup conditions. We integrated these results into an interactive OpenSpace visualization, allowing users to explore the Gale Crater and Earth locations through geographic overlays, camera navigation, and comparison dashboards.

TerraMatch makes environmental comparisons accessible and helps researchers identify useful locations for testing exploration technologies and preparing for future missions. It provides users with a customizable comparison matrix that measures the compatibility of Earth Analogs for Mars Missions. We envision TerraMatch helping scientists choose Earth testing locations for any future Mars Mission.
details:
TerraMatch combines NASA Earth-observation data with environmental measurements collected by the Rover Environmental Monitoring Station (REMS) aboard NASA's Curiosity rover at Gale Crater. We selected four Earth analog environments: the Aralkum Desert in Uzbekistan, McMurdo Dry Valleys in Antarctica, the Lut Desert in Iran, and Salar de Uyuni in Bolivia.

We collected daily meteorological data from NASA POWER spanning from 2015–2025 and processed Curiosity REMS observations from 2025, grouping measurements by Martian sol and calculating representative environmental averages. We developed a similarity index that compares Earth and Mars measurements across three categories: thermal, atmospheric, and environmental. We normalized the differences between measurements, combined them using a root-mean-square calculation, and applied an exponential similarity function. The resulting category scores are averaged to produce an overall comparative score in % for each location.

We integrated our analysis into OpenSpace, a NASA-funded interactive planetary visualization platform created by the American Museum of Natural History. Users can navigate between Mars and the four Earth analogs, explore geographic boundaries and 3D location markers, and view environmental comparison tables and similarity scores. The dashboard also supports selecting coordinates within the analog regions to retrieve NASA POWER climatology data and descriptive comparisons.

Our application uses Python for data processing and analysis, including NumPy and Pandas; HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the interactive dashboard; Lua assets and GeoJSON for geographic overlays and OpenSpace integration; and the OpenSpace JavaScript API for camera and interface controls. We incorporated NASA Earthdata EMIT for mineral data and ISRIC SoilGrids for soil pH, organic carbons, and bulk density, as supporting resources for examining surface characteristics. Google Gemini API provides AI-assisted contextual summaries and interpretations.

Our project brings quantitative environmental comparison into an interactive planetary exploration experience. Instead of treating one location as a perfect Mars equivalent, TerraMatch helps users understand where specific Earth environments resemble Mars and where important differences remain. This can help researchers identify potential field-testing environments for planetary exploration technologies, including rover systems, environmental sensors, and equipment designed for extreme conditions. Our longer-term vision is to expand the comparison framework to include additional geological, mineralogical, and topographical characteristics.

Please refer to our GitHub user guide for more explanation on Terraform’s capabilities and user interface. If you’d like to open Terraform on your computer, please see our GitHub install guide. Videos of the TerraMatch tours are provided in the Dropbox.
